description: Hello! We're Phantom6, a team of six students from the University of Information Technology (UIT), Myanmar. Although some of us are meeting for the first time, we're united by our curiosity, passion for building things. We're excited to explore how NASA's open data can be transformed into innovative solutions through the Fieldshift track. We're excited to see what we can create together.
summary:
Garvesty is a free web app that helps rice farmers in Myanmar's Ayeyarwady Delta decide what to plant in the dry season after the monsoon rice. Most farmers grow rice again by habit, even when water is short and the soil needs a break. Garvesty compares rice-to-rice against two cheaper pulse rotations, mung bean and black gram, for a specific field.
A farmer draws their field on a satellite map. The app refuses rivers, forested hills, towns and houses, using NASA MODIS land cover, Landsat-based surface water and OpenStreetMap buildings. It then builds the field's profile from NASA data: POWER weather, GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture and MODIS vegetation, plus SoilGrids soil. Six plain-language questions about priorities, weather worries, prices and resources lead to one recommended crop. The recommendation comes with reasons, a sowing window, published fertiliser rates and the source of every value.
It runs in English and Burmese, works offline, and includes a 3D season simulation and what-if scenarios. It never predicts yield or price, and it always labels satellite estimates as estimates. It turns NASA Earth data into a decision a farmer can act on and check.
details:
What it does

Garvesty helps Ayeyarwady Delta rice farmers choose a dry-season crop after the monsoon rice. It compares three rotations for a specific field: rice-to-rice (the usual practice, always shown as the baseline), rice to mung bean, and rice to black gram.

  1. Pick or draw a field. The farmer chooses an example field or taps the corners of their own on a satellite map. The app refuses a field that falls on a river, forested hills, a town or houses, and says why. Those checks use NASA MODIS land cover (500 m), JRC Global Surface Water from Landsat (30 m) and OpenStreetMap buildings.
    • NASA POWER: recent weather and temperature normals.
    • GPM IMERG: the last 30 days of rain, and monthly rain averages for 2001-2025.
    • SMAP: topsoil moisture.
    • MODIS: vegetation (NDVI).
    • ISRIC SoilGrids: soil pH and texture.
    • What-if scenarios: planting delay, drought, drainage or irrigation, recalculated on the spot.
    • A 3D field built in Blender, where a harvester cuts the rice and the chosen crop grows through the season on NASA climate averages.
    • A step-by-step analysis log.

Benefits and intended impact

Many Delta farmers repeat rice in the dry season by habit, even where water is short and pumping is costly. Pulses after rice need less water and little urea, and they break pest cycles. Garvesty makes that trade-off visible for one field, in Burmese, without needing a login, an expert or a constant internet connection. Extension officers can use it to start a conversation with a farmer, and it records what the farmer actually planted, which no satellite can see. In the long run that builds the local evidence a better model needs.

What we used

  • Data:
    • NASA: POWER, GPM IMERG (Late daily and Final monthly), SMAP (through AppEEARS), MODIS MOD13Q1 and MCD12Q1 (through the ORNL DAAC service).
    • Other sources: ISRIC SoilGrids, JRC Global Surface Water, OpenStreetMap, FAO EcoCrop crop ranges and Myanmar Department of Agriculture fertiliser rates.
    • Python with pandas, FastAPI and scikit-learn for the data pipeline and the main rules engine.
    • TypeScript, React and Vite for the app, with Leaflet maps and three.js 3D.
    • Blender for the 3D models.
    • The Python engine and its TypeScript copy are tested to give identical results, alongside 57 frontend and 39 backend tests.
  • Hosting: the app is published on GitHub Pages and runs fully in the browser, with no server.
  • Hardware: none. It runs on any phone or laptop browser.

What makes it creative

  • A map that says no: it won't let a farmer plan a crop on a river, a hillside or a house.
  • Advice built from the farmer's own answers and stated in their words, not a bare score.
  • A 3D season that turns weather averages into something a farmer can watch.
  • A trail on every answer showing which parts came from the farmer, the field and the satellite.

What we considered

  • Honesty: no yield, profit or price predictions. Climate averages are never called forecasts, and every estimate is labelled. We trained a soil-moisture model and tested 11 algorithms on sites the model had never seen. It didn't beat a simple baseline, so we left it out of the app and reported the result.
    • the crop rules still need review by a local agronomist
    • the Burmese wording still needs review by a native speaker
    • salinity data is not available
    • the house check covers only mapped areas near four towns
